Lemons are a nutrient-dense food known primarily as an excellent source of vitamin C, providing over half of the daily recommended intake in a single medium fruit. Compared to other daily foods, they are notably low in calories, fat, and sugar but high in beneficial plant compounds and fiber. 
Lemon Nutrition Overview
A medium-sized lemon (approx. 58 grams) contains approximately 17 calories and provides significant amounts of: 
Vitamin C: Over 30 mg, which is more than half of the daily recommended intake.
Fiber: Around 1.6 grams, mostly soluble pectin fiber that aids digestion and promotes fullness (found primarily in the pulp and peel).
Other Nutrients: Smaller amounts of potassium, folate, calcium, and vitamin B6.
Phytochemicals: Rich in flavonoids and limonoids, which are antioxidants with anti-inflammatory properties. 
Comparison to Other Daily Foods
Nutrient 	Lemons compared to Oranges	Lemons compared to Limes	Lemons compared to other Vitamin C foods
Vitamin C	Roughly similar in concentration per 100g, but oranges can be slightly higher depending on the serving size.	Contain about twice as much vitamin C as limes.	Good source, but other foods like guava or amla (Indian gooseberry) contain significantly more per 100g.
Calories/Sugar	Lower in calories and sugar than oranges.	Very similar low-calorie and low-sugar profile.	Lower in sugar than many common fruits like strawberries or kiwi.
Fiber	Contain less fiber than some other fruits, but the soluble fiber (pectin) content is notable when the pulp is consumed.	Similar fiber content to limes.	Generally good compared to many juices, but some other fruits like berries or kiwis are also great sources.
Minerals	Generally lower in minerals like calcium and potassium than oranges, but higher in iron and phosphorus.	Higher in potassium and magnesium than limes, but limes have slightly more calcium and phosphorus.	Provide only modest amounts of minerals compared to foods like dairy or leafy greens.

comments.text:
The post is from 4 May 2024: https://www.instagram.com/reel/C6j7Iz0yRfh/?igsh=a2VzYjE1NWowb3Zw

You say it's greasy, but you also call it a great/effective natural alternative to minoxidil in both the post and the caption ("Rosemary oil can be an effective natural alternative to minoxidil for many different types of hairloss. Essential oil needs to be diluted about 2 drops in 1 tsp of carrier oil. You can also buy it prediluted as hair oil. For best results use twice a day for 6 months.")

The problem with the benzene posts is that

A. The data you've based it on is likely inaccurate (see e.g. the Valisure FDA inspection letter, FDA announcements about benzene testing from last year, their close ties to class action lawyers, their previous testing has been found to be frankly incompetent) and 

B. chemophobia and exaggeration of hypothetical risks leads to exacerbating health anxiety unnecessarily, making choices that often increases risk, or increases cost unnecessarily, and bad policy. It also teaches people the logic of chemophobia, "Big pHARMa", beauty products don't undergo any toxicological assessments etc.

For example with benzene, the measured values from Valisure are likely hugely exaggerated, to the point where outdoor air could well result in higher benzene exposure than spraying indoors. Valisure have also weaponised the benzene contamination narrative to advocate for alternative benzoyl peroxide formulations which would increase patient costs for no actual benefit (similar to Andrew Wakefield/thimerosal).

People are also avoiding sunscreen because of exaggerated benzene concerns. In Australia there's been a huge surge in this narrative - several big influencers have posted reels about this that got millions of views (e.g. Jon Bernard). Having medical doctors endorse these narratives is particularly harmful, as you have the ability to sway otherwise pro-science audiences. 

Here's an article outlining the harms of chemophobia in more detail: https://news.immunologic.org/p/chemophobia-the-fear-of-chemicals

comments.author: @liveforlife2494
comments.text: I grew up with a mom who was and still heavily is into healthy lifestyles and more natural, less-processed foods and products of all kinds. A lot of us naturally feel better about using stuff that's "more natural" especially when we hear about common ingredients being bad for us, but from even just the little I've read into this, the "more natural" alternatives aren't always better and more effective for us. An example being that a lot of ingredients used as alternative to sulfates in sulfate-free shampoos haven't been resoundingly verified across the board as very safe for the general human population, if I'm remembering correctly. For things like shampoo bars, what I've read is that oftentimes these bars contain waxes (so the bar retains its shape) that don't wash away cleanly, which can actually create increased buildup on hair. I used to use shampoo bars myself for about 1-2 years and actually switched back to bottled products. My impression is that the science just isn't there yet to objectively say many of these "natural" alternatives are actually a better/safer choice. On the other hand, sulfates and also parabens have been proven repeatedly to be safe and effective. The whole "greenwashing" phenomenon is real and it feels good, of course, but it's also wise to consider if certain ideas we're told for or against certain types of products are, well, propaganda and fearmongering. Which is my long-winded way of saying, sending you solidarity from someone with a roughly similar background!

comments.text:
Hello, I want to share with you a very harsh reality we live in Paraguay.
Here, women do not always have access to contraceptives, and abortion is illegal even in cases of rape or when the mother’s health is at risk. This means that girls and women who have been raped are often forced to continue with the pregnancy.
Many women also die giving birth because they cannot legally access an abortion for medical reasons — even when their own lives are in danger.
In many cases, after giving birth, survivors of rape are unable to form an emotional bond with the baby, who then ends up being raised by relatives or abandoned. The child grows up feeling their mother’s rejection, and it is the child who carries that pain for life.

While researching female reproduction and pregnancy, I came across information about embryo absorption: a natural process in which, in some cases, the uterus reabsorbs the embryo. I know it sounds like science fiction, but I thought it could be an alternative to abortion.

I would like to try to find a way to make this absorption possible voluntarily and safely. If that were possible, the embryo would reintegrate into the mother’s body without the need for a surgical procedure or an invasive pregnancy termination.

Personally, I have mixed feelings about it, but I believe it could be a solution that does not break the law, and that could save many lives and prevent enormous suffering every day.

In my country, the stories I’m telling you happen frequently, and not all women have the resources or support to access contraceptives, let alone a safe abortion. I am looking for someone who could guide me or connect me with people interested in researching this kind of alternative.

If you have information, ideas, or interest in helping explore this possibility, please write to me — I would deeply appreciate hearing from you.

I just want to know if it could be possible. All contraceptive methods we have today did not exist in the past — and yet, now they do. So maybe, someday, this could be possible too.

I needed to share this because I believe we need to think about real and compassionate solutions for the women and girls who face these situations.

Thank you for reading.

"Some cultures have a belief about menstruation and the moon." It may have faded in modern times, but it's in our culture, too. "Menstruation" comes from "menses", which comes from the Latin word "menses", which is the plural of "mensis", which means "month", which came from the Greek "μήνη" ("méne"), which means "moon", or "μήν" ("mén"), which means "month", and all of this comes from PIE "menses" or "menes", which means "moon" and "month". Basically, "moon", "month", and "menses" are all the same word used in different contexts.

Not to imply that there's some sort of physical or metaphysical connection between a woman's cycle and the moon, of course.

comments.text:
Funny how the algorithm changes our medical opinions, isn't it, @DoctorMike?

It’s incredibly ironic to see you suddenly clutching your pearls over the Wim Hof Method when just a few years ago you were riding the wave with your own "100 Day Wim Hof Method Ice Bath Challenge."

You literally helped platform and popularize the guy to millions of your followers when it was trendy and lucrative. But now that the contrarian "debunking" pivot gets more engagement, suddenly the whole practice is a menace?

Let’s talk actual science, since we’re pretending this is about evidence-based medicine and not YouTube views:

The PNAS Study (2014): Researchers at Radboud University quite literally had to rewrite biology textbooks because Hof and his practitioners proved they could voluntarily influence their autonomic nervous system and innate immune response. The breathing technique spikes epinephrine, leading to a measurable increase in anti-inflammatory IL-10 and a decrease in pro-inflammatory cytokines. 

Wayne State University PET Scans (2018): Neuroimaging showed that the breathing and cold exposure directly activates the periaqueductal gray area (PAG) of the brain, promoting the spontaneous release of opioids and cannabinoids. That’s quantifiable pain suppression and stress regulation—not just a placebo.  

PLOS One Systematic Review (2023): Consistent findings across multiple trials show the method effectively reduces inflammation and regulates the sympathetic nervous system. 
 
It's completely valid to warn people not to force breathwork in a pool or push dangerously past their limits. But dismissing the entire peer-reviewed neurobiological mechanism just to farm contrarian clicks is intellectually lazy. Maybe stick to reacting to episodes of Grey's Anatomy and leave the physiological research to the people who don't need a ring light to read a PubMed abstract

comments.text: I really enjoyed this conversation. You say you wish you'd done a deeper dive into the facts, but I gained a lot of insight about how Scott Carney goes about his journalism and found that fascinating. My mother was a journalist in the 70s and we talked about ethics a lot, and bias, and trying to be objective. So the fact that the conversation wasn't specifically in the direction of strictly facts didn't bother me, because you also have to judge the quality of your information. I think Mr. Carney is spot on about looking at the past acts of the researcher and influences on them. I have to make judgement calls all the time when I look at scientific sources for my young adult science fiction writing. I do write fiction, but science fiction has to be based on fact, and more, on whether the extrapolations I make of the science are plausible, as things that could happen given the science that exists. Keep up the good work, Doctor Mike! I always learn a lot when I watch your content. When I have conversations with my current doctor and doctors I've had good doctor-patient relationships in the past, I always look for a doctor who's willing to say, I don't know. I'm 67 years old. I also do a lot of research in scholarly sources. So, I'm aware that science constantly changes when we discover new information over time. To me, it's a benefit when my doctor admits he or she doesn't know everything because no one can. I enjoy watching the process when my doctor explains what he or she does know, and what they're evaluating, and what they can't tell me. That process is what divides who I consider to be a doctor who's good for me as a patient from someone I'd rather not continue to see. Most doctors I've seen in my life have been on the 'good for me' side.

 Supermarket shampoos often used to be high in alkaline in the 70'-1990's in the late 90's this started to change. These days most respected haircare brands that have a pro salon range out and also produce a pharmacy and supermarket version are

comments.text:
Industrial Dairy Propaganda War On Raw Milk

The story of how homogenized milk came to dominate the market involves a concerted, early 20th-century campaign by industrial dairies to turn public perception against raw milk, utilizing propaganda, fear, and technical innovations to make raw milk appear dangerous, old-fashioned, and impure. This shift, often referred to as a "milk war," saw large-scale distributors battle small, independent farmers, ultimately changing the face of dairy consumption in America by the 1950s. 

Origins of the Conflict: Unsafe "Swill Milk"
In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, urban industrialization led to large-scale dairy farming in cities. Cows were kept in cramped, unsanitary conditions and fed the leftover byproduct of distillery grains, creating "swill milk" that was frequently contaminated with deadly pathogens like tuberculosis and typhoid. 
The Problem: Unsanitary urban conditions led to high death rates from diseased raw milk.
The Reaction: Rather than cleaning up the dairies, big dairy owners pushed for technological solutions to fix the diseased product. 
The Propaganda Campaign
To defeat independent, often cleaner, small farms, large-scale industrial dairy owners used wealth and influence to spread fear. 
Scare Tactics: Big dairy manufacturers ran "fake news" articles in popular magazines portraying all raw milk as dangerous, failing to differentiate between clean farm milk and urban swill milk.
Government & Private Alliances: Philanthropists, such as Macy's co-owner Nathan Strauss, partnered with industrial dairies to promote pasteurization through media campaigns.
The "Pure" Label: Industrial dairies marketed their processed, pasteurized milk as "Pure Country Milk" or "safe" milk, creating a false binary between their technologically altered product and "dangerous" raw milk. 
Homogenization as a Marketing Tool 
Homogenization—the process of breaking down fat globules so cream does not separate—was introduced in the 1930s not for safety, but for marketing and distribution convenience. 


The "Cream Top" Disadvantage: Raw milk naturally separates, with cream rising to the top. Industrialists used this against raw milk farmers, marketing the creamy layer as unsightly, old-fashioned, or "impure" compared to the uniform white color of homogenized milk.
Appearance of Uniformity: Homogenized milk looked consistent and processed, which gave consumers a false sense of security that it was "cleaner" or "safer," despite homogenization having no inherent safety benefits over pasteurization alone.
Extended Shelf Life: Homogenization allowed large dairies to ship milk longer distances, destroying local, small-scale dairy markets. 

The Shift in Marketing: "Got Milk?"
Following the successful, fear-based campaigns of the early 20th century, the late 20th century saw the "Got Milk?" campaign, which further solidified the dominance of standardized industrial dairy products. 

Generalizing the Product: The "Got Milk?" campaign was designed to promote milk in general, rather than specific brands, strengthening the collective power of large-scale industrial dairies.
Defeating Competition: This, combined with strict regulatory hurdles often advocated for by large dairy associations, effectively made the production and sale of raw milk legally difficult in many states. 

Legacy of the Campaign
The success of these marketing campaigns from the 1920s to the 1950s led to a lasting cultural stigma against raw milk. Today, despite a resurgence in interest, the majority of U.S. milk remains homogenized and pasteurized, with large dairy associations still heavily lobbying against the loosening of restrictions on raw milk sales.

BENEFICIAL PROBIOTICS IN RAW MILK

RAW MILK contains a diverse community of naturally occurring bacteria, particularly lactic acid bacteria (LAB), which are considered BENEFICIAL microbes that can AID DIGESTION, SUPPORT IMMUNITY, and PROMOTE a HEALTHY GUT microbiome. These PROBIOTICS are often DESTROYED by PASTEURIZATION. 
 
The most common and BENEFICIAL PROBIOTIC genera found in raw milk include: 
Lactobacillus species: L. plantarum, L. casei, L. fermentum, L. paracasei, L. rhamnosus, and L. helveticus. These are frequently identified for their ability to INHIBIT pathogens and IMPROVE gut health.

Lactococcus species: Lactococcus lactis is commonly found in raw milk and contributes to GUT BALANCE.
Leuconostoc species: Often present in raw milk and contributes to the biodiversity of the gut microbiome.

Streptococcus species: Streptococcus thermophilus is a primary, BENEFICIAL BACTERIUM found in raw milk that AIDS in GUT HEALTH.

Enterococcus species: Certain strains are found in raw milk and have shown PROBIOTIC POTENTIAL, though some can have pathogenic characteristics, requiring careful management.

Bifidobacterium species: These are often listed as part of the BENEFICIAL BACTERIA that can be found in raw, clean milk. 

KEY BENEFITS OF RAW MILK MICROBES 
LACTOSE DIGESTION: Many raw milk bacteria help produce the lactase enzyme in the gut, which can aid in breaking down lactose.
Immune System Modulation: Certain beneficial bacteria in raw milk can train immune cells and reduce allergies.

PATHOGEN INHIBITION: The naturally occurring lactic acid bacteria in raw milk produce metabolites that can INHIBIT the growth of HARMFUL bacteria, such as E. coli or Salmonella.

comments.author: @alta2732
comments.text:
Hi Kevin and Martin! I am currently a practising, board certified consultant surgeon (or an attending in the USA) in the UK who have dedicated my past 12 years in career progression (academic foundation, core specialty and subspecialisation in advanced surgery) and I had achieved the additional fellowship qualifications throughout the COVID pandemic to meet my advanced training needs. Both of you raised very important points which I do acknowledge and yet I must say that I share my issues with you both. 

Strictly speaking, Martin highlights that medicine (and surgery) requires extremely committed individuals to be the very best of their ability in those specialties- this includes lots of self-sacrifice in the service, zero personal enjoyment, zero weekend time, zero family time and to be on constant beck and call for any clinical need should it arise (e.g whenever the bosses summons you on very short notice). I was that individual fellow in those times during the fellowship. On one hand, I became a very committed surgeon with specialised skills and I can cope with pressure but I seriously lacked quality of life and enjoyment when I had free time coz my bosses still expect me to do more research, papers, additional reading and work-related activities on my downtime. The work does not stop at work- you bring it back home with its defeat and stress! In the patient's eyes and hospital eyes, I am a model employee and doctor as I care greatly for them and I can cope with loads of high pressure workload and complex cases. But on the flip side, I am rapidly burning out as a training surgeon but all of these hardships were expected at an advanced level of surgical (and medical) training in order to be able to manage complex cases independently. It seems to be a rite of passage to be a fully qualified board certified surgeon in the UK who can independently make decisions. I want to point out that without these forms of "whipping" and "tough love", lots of new consultants in the UK are facing difficulties managing challenging cases and are shaky when it comes a bit difficult to manage. 

As Kevin pointed out from his statements, we should all strive for financial literacy, work life balance, side hustle, other income streams and favourite lifestyle pleasures...which I completely agree as a current consultant surgeon and I had only wished I had done this back in my early days as a junior doctors. But with the increased training demands nowadays for training doctors, the new trainees are expected to do more and more work to meet the same milestone... it is unfair as postgraduate training takes up 99% of our youths and spouses/family/side hustle/personal enjoyment have to patiently wait for us to finish training to be able to enjoy family time. Yet, in today's time, the moment we finish training and become consultants, the hospital still expects you to be fully involved in care 24/7 which means there is no break to enjoy your life even at the consultant level. In addition, the NHS salary for UK consultant is appallingly low with little or no benefits of any perks or bonuses. However, if we were to completely embrace Kevin's lifestyle, where would we be with committed consultants and surgeons to manage the challenges in hospita;? We can just cut back at 5 pm due to time off and go off to home. We have to continue the surgery, continue the documentation and continue the management for our patients. 

In summary, Kevin's points are valid when it comes to having a life and enjoyment whilst being trained as a doctor. Martin's points are valid when it comes to being the best of the best among surgeons and physicians for our patients in order to be able to take on hard cases and challenging ones with adequate skills and experience. Putting in the reality check, I would cautiously adopt Martin's way as a trainee (70%) and then adopt more of Kevin's way of life as a consultant (90%). This would be my recommendations to future junior doctors.

comments.author: @TheTravisTube
comments.text: I think Dr Rutkowski makes some great points. More often than not, the "public faces" of certain medical fields on social media are less than ideal spokespeople for their profession. Suggesting that they may not be fully qualified to act in that role is simply Dr Rutkowski's opinion - and it's not "gatekeeping." Patients consume this material because it is highly accessible and often very entertaining, but infrequently supported or contextualized. For those reasons, laypeople SHOULD be skeptical of medical personalities online. Now a lot of this obviously depends on how much a person might be relying on the credibility that their degree affords them in the public eye, and what sort of content they are producing. I'm a medical doctor. You'll notice that there is no "M.D." behind my profile name, because that isn't what I do on YT. I'm not "Dr. Allen" to my friends; I'm only a doctor when I am working or when I am acting in a professional capacity. Now I don't have any problem with people who choose to put their titles on their social media profiles - that is entirely one's prerogative. But the Halo effect is rampant on YT, with physicians presenting information and laypeople willing to base the validity/competency on whether they think that person is attractive, shares their political views, or has a solid production. It should go without saying, but most of the real "influencers" in medicine aren't social media influencers at all - they aren't partying on yachts and reading startup company advertisements online - they are working diligently behind the scenes.

comments.text:
Great take! I just want to add a little something that you didn't cover which can give your audience a bit more nuance about Martin. 

Medicine is not monolith. Some specialties have more narrow definitions of positive outcomes while other specialties have outcomes that are difficult to measure. As a psychiatrist, the positive outcomes of my patients are very nuanced and hard to measure, hence I tend not to focus on binary measures but rather the patient's overall subjective wellbeing. Radiology for example, have narrower definitions of outcomes because things are literally in black and white. Clinicians in this field tend to adopt a more binary approach to their practice and professional development. 

I imagine neurosurgery is a form of precision medicine that prizes binary outcomes which may partly explain Martin's adoption of a binary worldview. Being able to deliver very specific results is how he measures his success as a surgeon, hence his obsession about separating facts from opinions. For example, removing a tumour is a fact (you can check the margins under the microscope) and not an opionin. 

But I also want to point out that he is an assistant professor, hence he speaks like an academic obssessed with P values and confidence intervals. 

I like to believe that Martin has a softer side to him, but my experience with neurosurgeons (or surgeons in general) tells me that most of them have a very similiar personality structure. They are usually not fantastic on an interpersonal level, and would rather let their work do the talking. Some doctors chose medicine specifically for this reason, and the field of medicine is large enough to accommodate people like this, especially in academia. 

I know professors who are borderline autistic with their patients but they produce some of the most amazing papers.

I'm currently in school as a pre-med and I agree with some of these issues that Dr. Martin is speaking about with the medical school influencers and how they inform you of what's going on. Nesse vídeo, o que o senhor fez foi dar uma opinião pessoal com base em dados científicos, o que a parte contrária também faz. Dados podem ser (re)contextualizados de diferentes formas a depender do discurso:
1) quando mencionou LDL, o senhor só afirmou que ele é sabidamente relacionado a problemas cardíacos e virou a página, quando, isoladamente, isso não é uma verdade. Existem cardíacos com LDL baixo e longevos com LDL alto, isso depende do tipo de LDL, ApoB, Lpa, inflamação... há um dado mundial de que quase metade dos infartados chegam ao hospital com colesterol "normal", dentro do valor de referência. 
2) Quando fala da crítica aos estudos observacionais, o senhor justifica isso pela inviabilidade ética de submeter indivíduos a uma dieta supostamente maléfica por décadas. OK, isso explica a inviabilidade mas não exime de inconsistência, como o senhor mesmo disse, ora o ovo faz mal, ora faz bem.
3) Quando fala do potencial carcinogênico da carne vermelha, foi num estudo que trocou carne processada por amêndoas, e não carne processada por carne. O que é cancerígeno, a carne ou os aditivos?

Ou seja, valorizou seus pontos e desprezou os contrários que são plausíveis. E não, eu não sou um "carnívoro" 😂, me recuso a pensar que essa imensa variedade gostosa e nutritiva de frutas, verduras, legumes, estejam aqui pra nos fazer MAL, mas o Dr não foi muito honesto dessa vez.

comments.text:
O Nick descobriu algumas coisas incríveis mas não é uma pessoa confiável. 
Ele descobriu que em várias pessoas magras com dieta cetogênica a gordura saturada não é o principal fator causando aumento do LDL. O próprio fenótipo magro em pessoas com dieta cetogênica causa aumento do LDL independente da ingesta de gordura saturada.
Pela medicina tradicional a gente espera que Oreos cause aumento do LDL por ser rico em gordura saturada mas o biscoito tirou ele de cetose e aumentou o peso. Ambas mudanças favoreceram queda do LDL e o efeito foi enorme. 
Ele também conseguiu induzir aumento do LDL em uma dieta cetogênica vegana pobre em gorduras saturadas.
Realmente é um mecanismo completamente diferente no controle do LDL que antes a gente não conhecia. A descoberta é incrível. A hipótese dele é que por ser um mecanismo diferente não necessariamente esse LDL alto seja fator de risco para infarto. Não havia nenhum estudo avaliando esse grupo, a própria composição desse LDL pode ser diferente do tradicional, é um questionamento válido. 
O próximo passo para testar essa hipótese foi o estudo para avaliar progressão de placa com angio TC. Ai que ele mostra a verdadeira cara. O desfecho primário do estudo não foi publicado !!! 
Tirando duas ou 3 pessoas todas as outras tiveram progressão de placa. 
A média de crescimento de placa foi semelhante a um grupo com escore de risco moderado a alto.
Considerando que é um grupo sem nenhum outro fator de risco o resultado foi catastrófico mas eles esconderam esse resultado para defender a dieta. A conclusão apresentada é uma análise secundária comparando progressão de placa do grupo com o próprio grupo que não faz parte do projeto original. 
O estudo é uma verdadeira vergonha, uma negação do método científico disfarçado de ciência.

comments.author: @physics4u2
comments.text: Prezado Dr. Carlos, sou inscrito no seu canal e aprecio a abordagem científica. No entanto, gostaria de ponderar sobre a relação entre o consumo de carnes processadas e o câncer colorretal, conforme divulgado pela IARC/OMS.É fundamental esclarecer que a IARC não afirma que o consumo de carnes processadas acima de 50g por dia causa câncer, mas sim que aumenta o risco. Analisando os dados matematicamente:A média de risco de desenvolver câncer colorretal na população geral, ao longo da vida, é de aproximadamente 4% (ou 40 pessoas em cada 1.000).O relatório da IARC (baseado primariamente em mais de 800 estudos observacionais, e não em ensaios clínicos controlados) indica que, para cada porção de 50 gramas de carne processada consumida diariamente, o risco relativo (RR) de desenvolver a doença aumenta em 18%. Aplicando este aumento ao risco absoluto :40x0,18 = 7,2. Isto significa um aumento de cerca de 7 a 8 casos adicionais por cada 1.000 pessoas, no grupo de maior consumo.Ou seja, o risco passaria de 40 para 47 ou 48 pessoas em cada 1.000.Portanto, o risco absoluto individual de desenvolver câncer colorretal devido ao consumo diário de 50g de carne processada é muito pequeno, embora o risco relativo seja de 18%. Essa distinção entre risco relativo e risco absoluto é crucial para evitar a desinformação e o alarmismo. Nem fiz os cálculos para a carne vermelha - porque os resultados beiram ao ridículo. Mas eu entendo que o alerta é feito para as pessoas que aderem a dietas extremas.

*Carne Processada:*

- É transformada para melhorar o sabor, textura ou durabilidade
- Pode conter aditivos, conservantes e outros ingredientes
- É frequentemente mais salgada e pode conter mais gordura
- Exemplos: salsichas, hambúrgueres, bacon, presunto

*Carne do Açougue (Carne Fresca):*

- É carne que não foi processada ou transformada
- É geralmente mais natural e contém menos aditivos
- Pode ser mais cara do que a carne processada
- Exemplos: carne de boi, carne de porco, frango, peixe

A principal diferença é que a carne processada é transformada para ter uma vida útil mais longa e um sabor mais intenso, enquanto a carne do açougue é mais natural e fresca

comments.author: @hugodacosta137
comments.text:
MENTIRA 1: “Dieta Carnívora tem menos de 20 estudos”

A VERDADE:
Ele está contando apenas estudos com o termo “carnivore diet”.
IGNORA:
- Milhares de estudos sobre dietas cetogênicas, low-carb e paleo
- Estudos sobre povos tradicionais (Inuit, Masai, Mongóis)
- Evidências arqueológicas e antropológicas

EVIDÊNCIA REAL:
- Estudos cetogênicos: +2.000
- Povos tradicionais: Centenas de estudos antropológicos
- Dieta paleolítica: Milhares de estudos
- Low-carb: +10.000 estudos

------------------------------------------------------------

MENTIRA 2: “Nossos ancestrais viviam 30 anos”

A VERDADE CIENTÍFICA:
- Expectativa de vida ≠ longevidade máxima
- Mortalidade infantil distorcia as médias
- Ancestrais que chegavam à idade adulta viviam 60–80 anos
- Fósseis mostram ossos de idosos bem preservados

EXEMPLO REAL:
- Ötzi (5.300 anos): Morreu aos 45, por assassinato
- Ancestrais que sobreviviam à infância tinham longevidade similar à nossa

------------------------------------------------------------

MENTIRA 3: “Ancestrais eram onívoros”

A VERDADE ARQUEOLÓGICA:
- Isótopos estáveis: mostram dieta predominantemente carnívora
- Tártaro dental: presença de plantas ≠ dieta baseada em plantas
- Anatomia humana: dentes, intestino e enzimas indicam adaptação carnívora

EVIDÊNCIA:
- Isótopos de nitrogênio: 70–80% da dieta era animal
- Plantas: 20–30% (tubérculos e frutas sazonais)
- Não eram agricultores — plantas eram complemento, não base

------------------------------------------------------------

MENTIRA 4: “Estudo de Harvard com 95% de melhoria é inválido”

A VERDADE SOBRE O ESTUDO:
- 2.029 participantes — número significativo
- 14 meses de duração — tempo adequado
- Dados autorrelatados: padrão em nutrição
- LDL 172: dentro da normalidade em vários protocolos

POR QUE ELE DISTORCE:
- Ignora que LDL isolado não prediz risco cardiovascular
- Ignora que inflamação é o verdadeiro fator de risco
- Desconsidera que HDL alto + triglicerídeos baixos = perfil protetor

------------------------------------------------------------

MENTIRA 5: “Experimento do Dr. Norwitz é inválido”

A VERDADE:
- N=1 é válido em medicina personalizada
- Dr. Norwitz é pesquisador respeitado
- Experimento controlado: mesmo indivíduo, mesmas condições
- Resultado: Óreos + carnívora > estatina mais potente

POR QUE FUNCIONOU:
- Eliminação de inflamação (sem carboidratos)
- Gordura saturada estabiliza LDL
- Cetose melhora o perfil lipídico

------------------------------------------------------------

MENTIRA 6: “Carne processada causa câncer”

A VERDADE SOBRE A CLASSIFICAÇÃO IARC:
- Grupo 1 = “Carcinogênica para humanos”
- Problema: baseada em estudos observacionais com grande viés

VIÉS:
Pessoas que consomem carne processada geralmente também fumam, bebem e são sedentárias.
Esses fatores confundidores não foram controlados.

EVIDÊNCIA REAL:
- Carne fresca: não classificada como carcinogênica
- Carne processada: risco vem dos conservantes, não da carne
- Estudos controlados: mostram benefícios da carne fresca

------------------------------------------------------------

MENTIRA 7: “Dieta carnívora causa deficiências”

A VERDADE NUTRICIONAL:
- Vitamina C: presente no fígado
- Vitamina B1 (tiamina): carne vermelha é rica
- Cálcio: em ossos, laticínios e peixes pequenos
- Fibra: não essencial (sem RDA estabelecida)

FATOS CIENTÍFICOS:
- Eskimos: viveram décadas sem frutas/vegetais
- Masai: dieta 80% animal, sem deficiências
- Inuit: dieta 90% animal, saúde excelente

------------------------------------------------------------

MENTIRA 8: “Dieta carnívora altera o microbioma para pior”

A VERDADE SOBRE O ESTUDO:
- 24 horas de análise — período muito curto
- Bilophila wadsworthia: bactéria normal em carnívoros
- Butirato: o corpo também produz
- Inflamação: reduzida com a dieta carnívora

EVIDÊNCIA:
- O microbioma se adapta à dieta
- Diversidade ≠ saúde
- O importante é a função bacteriana, não a quantidade

comments.text: @TheRejustine Quando há muita glicose circulando, a vitamina C não consegue entrar nas células com eficiência — ou seja, precisa-se de mais dela. comments.text: There is emergency exception if the subject is not breathing and will likely die without the procedure. The parents were right there and did not try to stop him, and there are enough witnesses to that fact. Though I know much of the show seems over the top, I have 2 boys on  the spectrum…a sixteen y.o.who is extremely spatially gifted, and a 21 y.o. who has graduated from high school but has no job and no prospects. Neither has ever passed the state assessments, but they are both communicative,make eye contact, and are intelligent in ways not meant to be celebrated in the education world.  I am blessed that my boys were in the school district where I worked as a teacher and where my ex-husband still works. I will say that Freddie did a remarkable job in his portrayal of the possible idiosyncrasies of a person with autism. If you’ve met one person with autism, well, you’ve met that one version of autism. You may never meet another person with all of the exact behaviors, aversions, comforts, speech patters, etc. I think it’s great that my boys have the option to see someone they recognize themselves in kicking ass and taking names…but that’s just me!

4:45 as an art student, not a doctor of any sort, but someone who has severe adhd and therefore thinks about how their brain works a lot, I believe it is caused by your brain focusing on facial features and when those facial features are suddenly changed your brain attempts to apply the same proportions as the previous face to the next one. but since people have different facial structures and proportions, it makes the faces look distorted or  "wrong". The reason it only works with two images at once while focusing in between them, is because if it were only one picture you wouldn't rely on peripheral vision which is blurrier requiring your brain to have to work harder to identify a face and your attention isn't being split by trying to focus on the cross and looking at both faces at the same time which slows your brains reaction time and processing speed by overloading your senses with new information

In short, your brain uses the previous images to help identify the features of the next image and when the features of the next image don't match, your brain thinks there's something "wrong" with the face

comments.text:
"How do they know when they act all the time" Well, first and foremost understand that the refs are not just there for show.  They are wrestlers themselves, often pulled from local wresting federations for the road shows, and they do know how things are supposed to be done and can quickly see a blown spot.  There is always various communication, verbal and non-verbal that the wrestlers can share with each other and with the ref to indicate issues.  

One of the biggest telltale signs for how you know a real, and not fake, injury has happened is when you see the ref or the opponent cross their arms in an X towards the backstage.  That is an immediate "we have a real injury that requires medical attention now" sign.  This is one of the things, for safety reason, they will not fake.  They never want to confuse the medics with a fake signal.  The Randy Orton shoulder separation video you can see the ref doing the X showing that he needs medical attention.

comments.author: @BeeMcDee
comments.text:
Ah, the days when the most deadly thing at Bondi was a jellyfish…

All the same, I’m grateful this video came up on my feed. I’m Aussie, and this helps me remember what we value. Thank you. ❤️

These guys ARE actually qualified to observe what’s happening,  provide first responder intervention, and pass the info on to the paramedics. In more recent times, I think one of the lifeguards is actually a paramedic. When you call the ambulance here, they always ask what’s happening and what medical conditions you might have that are relevant.

ETA: the wheelchair user guy who has diabetes and epilepsy… yes I agree that they maybe should call an ambulance just in case (he might have refused it because ambulances aren’t free in most states and you have to have a membership, otherwise it costs upwards of $900), but the shaking and/or slurring could be from any one of those conditions. If he has a high-level acquired spinal injury — which I’d say he does because he’s got no grip strength and the characteristic  ‘paunch’ common for people with spinal injury — he could be shaking from that. In addition, a hypoglycaemic episode causes you to shake and slur your words, which is probably why al he can get out is ‘drink, drink’. The best thing they can do for him is to give him glucose while he’s conscious, bring him out of his chair and put him in the stable side position in case he has a seizure before the ambulance comes.

How do I know? I have all 3 conditions also.

I started a meth addiction around 2001, in 2005 I was arrested, convicted, got probation. It was pretty devasatating. Afer the probation was over, i went back to the drugs again, but was utter depressed. The appetite suppression effect had long since gone away. comments.text: I am so glad I stumbled onto this clip!  I too am facing challenges in addressing my own obesity and it *is* a complex, multi-faceted situation.  Finding and keeping the right support crew (medical, social, familial, whatever) is crucial to success.  As is the right attitude from the person suffering from obesity.  It's a daily struggle seeing this you and wondering how the hell did I get here!?  How do I get back to what I was and regain the benefits of *not* carrying this surplus weight around.  Your talk about exercise resonated hugely - I tried to return to walking but found the back pain excruciating.  I am with a new doctor and we are in the early stages of establishing baselines of what's going on before formulating a plan for moving forward.  I remain optimistic and confident of success but am not deluded about what it will take to get from A to B.  Thank you so much for your gentle, kind but straight up shared knowledge and comments.  It really does make a world of difference and provide a wonderful morale boost.  All the best and thanks again =)

comments.text:
I love what you said about thinking in scale and writing things down to look back on to view progress. This can apply to all faculties of life! Learning a new skill? Write what you struggle with and what you hope to improve, and do that each day. In a few weeks, look back and see how far you’ve come. This can be used for recovery from chronic illness, job improvement, learning a language, deepening faith, etc.

I’ve been doing this with my faith journey (prayer journaling), recommended by a good friend.  I started journaling a few months ago when my family was going through a tough time with both job loss and infertility. I wrote to God what I was struggling with and what I prayed would improve, giving thanks for what I have and what He’s given me. Now, our situation is much improved, and miraculously, I’m currently 12 weeks pregnant with a baby we never expected (but always hoped) would happen. It’s been truly amazing to look back in my journal and see all the prayers God has answered, and all the growth I’ve experience in just that time.

Just goes to say, journaling is amazing for all aspects of life, and it changes your perspective. Whether you’re trying to lose weight, train for a sport, create a new healthy habit, or in my case, strengthen faith and build hope. You won’t regret it!

comments.author: @Damiana_Dimock
comments.text:
Pretty sure that was Adin Ross, and he’s def got more wrong w/ him than just his eyes.

Some of these clips reminded me of when Hasan Piker & co. went to China, great streams great trip overall, but one of the places they visited was some some sort of traditional medicine facility, (you could tell they weren’t not really sure what to expect, that it was something placed on their itinerary and they said, “sure, let’s check it out.” 

While the martial artistry they showed them was cool and the chiropractor type stuff was pretty typical even for us in the west, it was definitely one of the most annoying & eyeroll-inducing parts of the trip when they got their consultations and a guy was like “stop drinking iced water,” and they were like, “we don’t.” No matter how hard they tried to make the stream entertaining because they knew most of us were not having it, they also had to balance out some general respect—That whole segment ended up being pretty awkward.

We’re all pretty inundated with vague references to “toxins” at this point, and I think most people who are watching this video all have the same general sense that it’s nonsense unless you provide any kind of evidence for your claims about them, what really got me here is the potato video. I love folklore, witchcraft, magick, even stuff like astrology, but I also have a form grasp of the scientific method and get my blood work done when I can. So when I see someone who does these sorts of folkloric home remedies and genuinely appears to believe them at face value, it makes me sad.

I mean, that’s not really what these practices are really meant to do—If you’re living in a cabin in the woods, à la The VVitch, having a mother do something and tell their child, “it’s going to be okay,” helps them stop worrying and go to sleep—Because they need the sleep, and clever women of the past used the darkness of the potato as a way to tell a story to the child, and comfort them, etc. 

A hard lesson for people to learn, (in part because of how we teach history,) is that the people of the past were not dumber than the people of today, there were smart people and dumb people then as there are today, and some just understood bed-side manner better than others, they understood child psychology, (in a less academic way, absolutely, but so do many childcare professionals today.) Those are parts of belief systems that are not supposed to make it past childhood, so I wonder if that mother does the potato thing for herself as well, or just for the child.

5:37 - Acupuncture sore throat trick.

During my practice as an Acupuncturist, I personally did not find needling the Jing Well points to be effective for sore throats. (Jing Well points are those demonstrated in this video on the finger and toes at either the end or beginning of the Qi meridians). 

HOWEVER, there was one technique which worked almost instantaneously EVERY TIME on patients with raging, burning throats.  I additionally used the technique multiple times on myself and the relief was immediate. 

The patient needs to press their tongue firmly to the roof of the mouth, exposing the two lingual veins under the tongue. Using a triple pointed needle, lance the underside of veins until a tiny amount of blood is released.

It worked EVERY TIME, and used to stun the patients. And no, it doesn't hurt if the tongue is under pressure and the lance is sharp. Just two "pops" and sore throat relief. 

As well has having been an Acupuncturist in the 1990's, working in conjunction with medical doctors, I went on to study a BAppSc, my major being in Biochemistry, with minors in physiology and molecular biology. I also have postgraduate qualifications in Nutrition. So I have walked the line between Alternative Medicine and Science. 

Modern scientific research explains Acupuncture's local and centralised pain numbing via the concept of Diffuse Noxious Inhibitory Control (DNIC) which involves using a peripheral painful stimulus to attenuate existing, more intense pain. 

Scientific research has also demonstrated the release of endogenous opioids, Neuro-Immune Interactions and an increase substance P, calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), and adenosine, which play a role in both local and central pain modulation. 

So, I suggest that before you post an immediate click bait YouTube dismissal, that you first review the peer-reviewed,  scientific literature

Soon after, i had to use the bathroom. ALL the older ladies pushed me to the head of the line so i did not have to wait. I was in late second trimester and no doubt about it. ALL the older women were all smiles as i continued out of the bathroom, thanking me. . 

A sweet fun memory. I think of that bride and hope she has had a good life.

comments.text: Corrections after looking it up more, I can only find one instance of this ever resulting in a viable pregnancy (boy born in 1995) and that was because the cells essentially piggy backed off a normal fertilized pregnancy. They can cause this division in a lab (called parthenogenesis ) to create embrios for research and such but they're not viable. It's so dangerous to try bringing them to term it's banned to try implanting a person with them. Usually if this occurs naturally it just becomes a tumor because a viable embrio requires two sets of DNA for the essential genes to activate (which I assume is nature's check to prevent this exact thing from happening in mamals). So basically, I stand by the assessment that they need to talk about all the possibilities and especially a plan for monitoring the mother very closely and prepare for what to do if(when) it goes bad to avoid as much harm to the mother as possible. comments.text: Don't jump to blame the lab! I worked 40+ years in a clinical lab and saw way too much. The worst ever was a patient in ER that  the Doctor requested a repeat on a couple of tests. The repeat sample wasn't even close to the original results. Extremely angry Doctor noises and two more samples that still did not match. I collected all four samples and headed to blood bank. In less than fifteen minutes, I determined that there were three different blood types among the four samples. I went to the Lab director and we sent one of our own phlebotomists to draw samples. When they returned, we discovered that the original patient had never had blood drawn until our lab person arrived. FOUR times the wrong people had blood drawn. Big executive meeting the next day. I personally observed on multiple occasions, ER personnel draw blood samples from multiple patients, place tubes in different pockets, then walk back to the main station. Once there, pockets were emptied into piles and tunes were THEN labeled. Even after the administration implemented "foolproof" patient ID and labeling policies, we still had issues with mislabeled samples. Apathy and overwork can always find work arounds for any system. All hospital personnel are human and make mistakes. Always ask questions and demand answers. Patients can always ask for second opunions.

that being said, yeah it's just a show, but i at least think it's a testament to strong character writing that he feels so real it's easy to imagine his life off-screen!

comments.text:
3 years ago... Yeah, but I am binging again and I missed this one... So... I went in because I was having issues with vertigo and we were looking at a possible pinched nerve in the neck. My PT did (I forget what it's called) the pen test where you follow it with your eyes and he discovered something he thought was wild. "Um, I have never seen this before! What the heck? Wait, you have a neurologist right? 'Cause ah.... Hey let me do that again, I got to see that again. Okay?" Then he told me that he was going to step out and consult a colleague. 

Ten minutes later he and his colleague knock on the door. "Hey, so... Do you mind if I do that test again?" I shrug because like I am so used to my body doing weird stuff I might as well. New doc, explained to me as a neuro type, stares at me and kind of smiles a bit. "Oh! I think I know what this is! But I've never seen it in real life before! I'll be right back." 

I get to have small talk with PT neck doc for about ten minutes and I decide I want to see so he repeats the test while filming with my phone. What did I see? So, both eyes are concentrated on the pen until he starts pulling it towards my face my right eye gives a little wiggle then goes off on it's own into a straight forward position like it decided to suddenly give up. I had to watch it several times. 

Neuro dude comes back in and says, "I know what this is!" Yeah, they were both very excited and I say, "Can we fix it? And is it causing my vertigo?" Sort of, I have to do PT for the rest of my life. Basically, I have to retrain the disconnection between my brain and my eye by doing PT exercising a few minutes a day. Yes, it's helped but if I stop it goes back to disconnecting again. Is it the cause of my vertigo? Um, kinda. But... I have a chiari malformation so... Who the heck knows... Medicine is a science and ever changing and the brain is something we still need to know a lot more about. Okay, story over... Sorry if I bored you!

comments.author: @Kohchu
comments.text:
Honestly, the amount of torment Marv and Harry go through in this movie is absurd. But that's what makes it funny; A normal person would go "Okay, I'm getting hurt... this is no longer worth it, this was supposed to be easy. I didn't sign up for this; tactical retreat." But these two turn their attention away from the original goal; Robbing the house, and instead focus on getting revenge on the little brat responsible. In doing so, they sustain:

- Harry: Shot in the groin by a BB Gun
- Marv: Shot in the Forehead by a BB Gun
- Marv: Slip and fall on Ice
- Marv: Crowbar to the back of the head (It falls off the door)
- Harry: Slip and fall on Ice
- Marv: Branding Iron to the face (Note: Common misconception - It wasn't plugged in or hot, but it's still an iron to the face).
- Harry: Burn wound to the Hand from heated Doorknob, and instantly freezing it in snow.
- Harry: Slip and fall while desperately trying to cool his hand.
- Marv: Nail to the foot.
- Marv: Fall from the 8th stair to the ground.
- Harry: Blowtorch to the head, and instantly freezing it in snow.
- Marv: Slip and fall on Ice again (he forgot it was there).
- Marv: Walking through Snow barefoot (This can actually cause a lot more damage than one might think due to frostbite).
- Marv: Stepping on Christmas Ornaments (Glass)
- Harry and Marv: Slipping and falling due to Hotwheels cars.
- Harry and Marv: Paint cans to the face, and impact from the Stairs to the ground. (Note: The cans likely aren't full, as Kevin wouldn't be able to lift them if they were, but they are still enough to do some damage).
- Harry and Marv: Trip and fall by a tripwire. (Harry takes the full fall, Marv tries to jump it and manages to grab Kevin while taking the dive).
- Harry: Crowbar to the ribs (Friendly fire while trying to kill Buzz's Tarantula).
- Harry and Marv: Falling from the top floor of the mansion as Kevin cuts the wire from the house to the Treehouse
- Harry and Marv: Impact to the wall and fall to the ground.
- Harry and Marv: Bashed on the Head by a shovel. (Not Kevin's trap, but hey; still an injury).

And that's just from the first movie. I'm not even going to include the ones from the second movie.

comments.text: I actually get hiccups on a regular basis due to stomach issues- heart burn. Anyway- the thing I've found that helps is to take a deep breath, hold it, this pushes against the diaphragm and sort of holds it in place, keeps it from spasming- I hold it as long as I can and then slowly release the pressure- and try to calm yourself while doing it, close your eyes, turn off any sound, etc. This sort of interrupts the hiccups and they go away, works for me anyway. At least it usually does anyway- sometimes nothing helps, I just have to wait them out. I can tell when that's the case because they won't stop even while I'm holding my breath, no matte how much pressure I put on my diaphragm. You have to do more than just hold your breath really- you take a deep breath and then push down on it- which sounds odd but is really easy to do. You've got your lungs full, you just get air in your mouth and try and push it into the lungs- not hard, just enough to make them expand and push against the diaphragm that's right underneath them- that's what is spasming and causing your hiccups.

comments.author: @jontastic
comments.text: I helped implement an EMR when they first started becoming available. Many doctors used typing apps to learn how to do that. Now every chart is readable and available on demand from every location across the region, and even shareable electronically anywhere on the planet. These notes can and are used for research, for accurate billing, and more. Prior to that, vans would go to the central chart complex and pull the charts then deliver to the hospital or clinic prior to the patient’s arrival. Much better for everyone, except the extra typing of the doctors. Although standard and custom templates are used to fill in the blank to reduce that load.

وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِي عَنِّي فَإِنِّي قَرِيبٌ ۖ أُجِيبُ دَعْوَةَ الدَّاعِ إِذَا دَعَانِ ۖ فَلْيَسْتَجِيبُوا لِي وَلْيُؤْمِنُوا بِي لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْشُدُونَ.
(سورة البقرة، الآية ۱۸۶ )
إن كنتم تطلبون جسدًا سليمًا، وروحًا مطمئنّة، وشخصيةً قويّة، فتوجّهوا إلى هذه الرسالة. فكلّ إنسانٍ يعود إلى هذه الدنيا وهو مزوّد بمصدرٍ من القوّة والطاقة الإلهيّة، غير أنّ هذا المصدر قد يضعف مع مرور الزمن، وبسبب مشكلات الحياة وصعوباتها، فيتحوّل إلى أمراضٍ جسديّة ونفسيّة وروحيّة.
اقرأوا القرآن الكريم بلغتكُم الأم لمدة تسعة عشر يومًا، وشاهدوا تجلّي الإعجاز في حياتكم. وخلاصة أربعةٍ وثلاثين عامًا من التجربة، والتعلّم على أيدي معلّمي النور، ومشاهدة آلاف المعجزات من القرآن الكريم عبر تلقّي قوّة الله في حياة الآخرين، تتجلّى في الدخول إلى عالم المعجزات والملكوت، والولادة من جديد، والتحرّر من العبثيّة والضياع، والحصول على إجابات لأسئلتكم، والتعويض عن السنوات الضائعة من حياتكم، والنموّ والنضج الفكري، والتكامل الروحي، وإزالة الفقر المادي والروحي، والتخلّص من الشعور بالذنب، والشك، والتشاؤم، وانعدام الأمان، والخوف من المستقبل، والوحدة، والوسواس، وعدم النجاح، واكتساب الثقة بالنفس بقوّة الله، والشفاء من جميع أنواع الأمراض والإدمان، والعثور على المفقود، سواء كان إنسانًا أم أشياء.
الأَمَةُ المؤمنة بربّ العالمين
السيّدة فاطمة روحاني

comments.text: You are far from alone.  I mean, this video has 12 million views!  I've thought about your question for a very long time, since my mom was removing zits for me over fifty years ago so here's my two cents worth.  The idea I've come to think fits well is that this kind of caring for another person must trigger something pleasing deep in our nature.  We see wild life videos of monkeys, apes, and other primates grooming each other.  In these documentaries it appears that grooming brings relief to the one being groomed and satisfaction to the groomer.  Almost like one creature is saying to another 'I care about your health and comfort and I'm taking care of you".  I'm not saying we're just like these animals only that since we are built on a similar blueprint that 'grooming' might affect us similarly deep down inside.  I'm not claiming any scientific certainty or authority.  It just looks like we're not so different from other members of the animal kingdom to me.  I don't think you're weird at all.

The thing with looking at a bright light to "ignite" a sneeze is real. If you feel like you have to sneeze but cannot, it's kinda annoying. You want to sneeze or not, not be stuck in "sneeze limbo". I read this in a medical article  somewhere but I can't remember exactly how it works. It has something to do with nerves, kinda like how smell triggers memories but with a different nerve to trigger the sneeze.
EDIT: I've tried this myself and it does indeed work. Next time you feel like you have to sneeze but can't, try it. The light has to be very bright though. Almost blinding. Look directly at a lamp or light bulb. Look towards the sun (not directly at the sun duh) just to get some very bright light to enter your eyes. Or if you are indoors on a very sunny day, just walk outside. This may be enough. Ever sneeze as soon as you walk outside on a sunny day? Might have had a sneeze hiding the whole time! Also, I know this entire thing is no big deal and has no impact on anything. I just find it interesting and a cool bit a medical knowledge.

comments.author: @Kat-d9y
comments.text: Man, I am such and old nurse.  When I started as a nursing student at small hospital, IV bottles and heavy plastic tubes were what we used.  To put in an IV all we had were straight metal needles, no soft flexible needles.  No IV pump, we learned to calculate added medications and count the drops per hour.  I remember when we got our first MA 1 ventilator.  On the night shift, no pharmacist, no respiratory therapist, no radiologist.  We did not even have an ER.  The night RN Supervisor triaged any admissions.  We of course did not get ambulances.  The staff nurse (me) acted as the pharmacist running to the pharmacy to get needed medications. I acted as the respiratory therapist, giving IPPB treatments, checking on the ventilators and there was no such thing as an emergency X-ray.  When we first got an on call staff doctor it was amazing.  The doctors did have to be awakened and drive into the hospital.  I had to learn to intubate, set up the ventilator, and know when to call the on call doctor.  What an amazing change in just 50 years.

comments.text:
I was born with a rare condition called Madelung’s deformity. At age 12, I underwent reconstructive surgery on both wrists—plates, screws, and even a small bone graft from my hip to help fuse everything together. Thankfully, there was an orthopedic hand and arm specialist in my city who could take on the challenge.

A couple of years later, my body rejected the hardware, and I had it all removed. That surgeon truly gave me my life back—without those procedures, I would have likely been paralyzed in both arms by my late teens or early 20s.

Now at 30, I’m living a normal life! It’s amazing how doctors can completely change the course of someone’s future, especially when dealing with rare conditions like this.

Dr. Mike, have you ever come across Madelung’s deformity? I’d love to hear your thoughts—and by the way, I love your videos! ❤🩺

comments.text:
I feel like the anti-lions mane answer was a bit to negative-affirming. 
Yeah the lions mane coffee thing is sensationalist.

But the studies on mice and cell cultures are very promising. Eating lions mane and its effects on brain health are simply not studied or incompletely studied. We use mice and cell cultures to guide further study, and toxicity studies of lions mane show that it is safe to eat in comparative quantities as staple foods. 
Consuning lions-mane mushrooms in the hope that it will benefit brain health is NOT pseudoscientific or anti-scientific. Claiming that it has specific benefits for humans is, but experimenting or supplementing(keyword supplement, as in addition to) is fine, and possibly, but not certainly, beneficial.

There IS evidence that it benefits human cells, even if those are cell cultures. I find her mentioning that cells are "grown on a piece of plastic" as pretty unprofessional and reductionist, especially as a biomedical researcher, as PEGylated plastics are some of the most important tools in biomedical research involving tissue engineering. The evidence provided by cel culture studies of lions mane mushrooms are incredibly encouraging toward future experimentation. 
I agree that the labels on LM coffee are sensationalist and anecdotal claims of increased focus arenot data.

But they aren't anti-hypothetical, and the evidence of lab cultures and murine models means that supplementing lions mane to help brain health is perfectly rational. Once we actually have short and long term clinical studies on humans, then we'll know for sure. 
A doctor saying "in addition to the gold standard of treatment ive prescribed for you, you may want to consider lions mane supplements, as it has been indicated in pre-clinical studies to have benefits on brain health." wouldn't be causing any harm, acting irrationally, or misleading patients on their course of treatment. 

Tldr, she's way to harsh on the lions main mushrooms thing, and acting like cell culture studies arent evidence is reductive and unprofessional

comments.text:
OCD sucks. I suspect I’ve had it my whole life, but was formally diagnosed at the beginning of this year. My therapist has been a godsend and I recommend therapy for everyone. I went into it not sure if it works, but it does. I always thought I was just insecure with how much I worried, notably about relationships. But when it got to the point where I had an intrusive thought that simply said “you don’t love your girlfriend” and it didn’t seem to have any valid rhyme or reason, it was so debilitating and scary. I spent hours and hours each day ruminating, trying to win the argument. Even though I knew it wasn’t true, the thought came from me, so sure it must have been true. Got bad enough to the point where I had to call out from work cause I was a wreck, and ended up taking some sleeping medicine (a safe amount) just so I could sleep and not have to be with the pain. 

Or times where I thought I was exposed to ocular herpes because someone that I knew had it sneezed around me and I thought a drop hit my face. Even though I knew it was so incredibly unlikely, I felt so controlled by the thought. And even felt forced to use some hand sanitizer as a form of lotion on my face near my eyes. It burned but was the only way I felt somewhat relieved from the thoughts. And even then, that night when I got home, I was a wreck from the constant panic, worrying, and ruminating. 

There’s a whole lot more to it, but all that to say that when it gets bad, it’s really bad. 

What helped me was therapy and some medication. The therapy helped me learn how to recognize the moments when they came up, and how to manage them with meditation or grounding exercises. The medication helped take the edge off of the worst moments where they seem to either come much further in between or not near as bad.

I used to one of the people that would be like “oh I’m so OCD”, and while it doesn’t offend or really bother me when people use it loosely, I’ve definitely grown a firsthand understanding of how bad it gets.

keep your hope and faith. i struggle with debilatating cycles of ocd compulsions / obsessions sometimes lasting up to 2 days at a time, pushing my body and brain to the brink of its limits. putting my life and health , both physical and mental at risk of failure for those loops. for those two days, the longest i have been in a loop of ocd cycles / relentless compulsions and obsessions, or trances, i will go 2 days in that loop of endless panic without sleep and much food, almost like in a trance that i usually cant get out of. in that time i will be in my head cycling through compulsions, almost unaware of time in a trance like panic and trying to stay above water and get to the other side. catching eyesight of the alarm clock, out of the corner of my eye every so often by chance and realizing how many hours have gone by since the last time i saw the clock. usually about four hours at a time every glance. it is the hardest thing i have ever endured. i literally try to tell myself and make myself stop doing compulsions, and saying this will be the last compulsion, knowing that i am on the brink of losing my mind, and then literally being unable to stop. i go into shock i guess. i dont know what to do when i get to that point, but to keep doing compulsions until i am able to get the miracle of a reprieve however / whenever that may be. i notice that if and when i do get to that miracle point of a reprieve and moment of rest, both physical and mental and temporary clarity of mind and peace, - that that is my one chance then to get the strength and courage and motivation and determination i need to start back the erp and therapy cycle. i need to get back on the right track of erp and therapy/ recovery as soon as i possibly can, and remember to myself that if and when i do give in to my ocd again, every time, every bit of attention or acknowledgement or compulsion or act of avoidance i do and participate in, the harder it is to going to be able to get back to that point of rest / sense of clarity / seeminly sanity / and  peace again. if it is ever even attainable again, that is the risk i take every time i choose to do a compulsion and step farther away from that recovery mindset. that recovery mindset / state is extremely precious and valuable and can be gone again in an instant if it is not protected and strengthened and nourished constanstantly by every choice choice I make by doing my recovery / erp therapy. keep the door to your ocd closed. and everytime time you might give into your ocd or compulsion just know that you are at risk of losing your peace again, possibly forever. value it.

  i have to have hope though, and faith because if i dont have that in the back of my mind, even if i cant see it or feel it, or realize it, then what do i have? its the only thing that gives me a chance at recovery and remission from this debilitating chronic lot of an anxiety disorder i have been delt.

goodluck. i hope you dont give up. i am constantly trying not to myself as well every day.

peace be with you

we have got this.

comments.text: I've had OCD (clinically diagnosed) for 34 years. Here's what helped me besides medications: remember anxiety is addictive to the brain. The more you obsess and focus your attention on all that can go wrong, you're going to find more anxiety & worry. It'll never be completely gone, but it's not as loud if you stop yourself mid-worry & tell yourself "STOP!" & then immediately think another thought to replace it. Whether it's the anxiety 3 rule, where you look around & name 3 things you see, 3 you hear & 3 parts of your body, etc. Or something all together different. This has taken me a few decades to learn through therapy. I hope it helps anyone reading this! You're stronger than you think you are!!!! 🫂

Key pillars of her day-off routine include:

•	Prioritize & Plan (01:24 - 03:16): Faye uses a 'brain dump' and the Eisenhower Matrix to clear mental clutter and reduce decision fatigue by categorizing tasks based on urgency and importance.
•	Brain Juice (03:17 - 04:19): She emphasizes that exercise is non-negotiable, noting that it boosts Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF), which enhances memory, focus, and executive function.
•	Pamper & Prep (04:20 - 06:00): A structured self-care session, including dry brushing and specific hair/skin routines, which serves as a reset for her physical appearance and well-being.
•	Mind Over Matter (06:01 - 07:29): She replaces passive consumption (like watching reality TV) with active learning through platforms like Skillshare to improve cognitive flexibility.
•	Matcha Before Mayhem (07:30 - 08:39): Faye opts for matcha over coffee, explaining that the L-theanine content provides a calm, focused alertness without the typical jitters or energy crashes.
•	Midday Reset (08:40 - 13:15): She incorporates mindfulness and meditation to combat midday energy dips and lower cortisol levels, helping her stay present during stressful or high-stakes moments.
•	Push & Rest (13:16 - 13:59): By tackling her most important tasks early via the Eisenhower Matrix, she can fully 'switch off' in the evening, establishing firm work boundaries to improve sleep and reduce rumination.
•	Quality Time (14:00 - 14:45): Ending the day with focused, meaningful social interaction to boost oxytocin and reconnect with what matters most.

I apologize if this post is long, but if you cannot bear to read it for 180 seconds, know that this has been happening in a part of this Earth for 80 years. Let’s set aside those 80 years and focus only on the last two.
In just two years:
Over 79,220 Palestinians have been martyred, not including those in Lebanon, or the bodies that vanished and turned to ash. The occupation uses thermal vacuum explosives reaching temperatures of 3500°C or more, incinerating human bodies into ash within seconds. If you cannot fathom the horror of these numbers, think if someone you love had just a single hair on their head harmed—only then will you understand.
Death is not the end in Palestine. Many bodies are blown up again after being buried; others are stolen for organ trafficking and then tossed in the trash as remains stuffed with cotton.
Hundreds of children have been kidnapped and tortured with electric shocks, cigarettes, and sharp instruments boring into their flesh. I am not talking about young men; I am talking about children under the age of five.
Gaza has seen mass graves defined by numbers. They were denied the right to be known by their names; they were treated as mere digits without value.
Gaza was starved. Food, water, medicine, feminine hygiene products, and anesthesia were all blocked. Amputations are performed on children and adults with no anesthesia whatsoever.
Thousands are suffering from skin diseases and viral infections, while 2 million people have been displaced dozens of times, only to drown in rain inside canvas tents.
Thousands of children are now orphans, some without even a family record left.
The Zionist entity has broken hundreds of truces. They blocked aid, and when they finally allowed some in, it was luxury coffee and chocolate—useless against famine. To put it simply: they are mocking our hunger.
For months, Palestinians couldn't even find flour. A single loaf of bread became a dream.
The occupation claims to punish Hamas, but I do not understand how a month-old infant can be "affiliated with Hamas" or carry a weapon to be killed in cold blood.
Palestinians are attacked by military dogs, including a child with Down syndrome and an elderly woman who had no strength to resist.
Thousands of journalists and paramedics were killed without justification.
Dozens of schools and universities were bombed. There are no schools left, and tragically, there are almost no students left—most have been martyred.
12,958 Palestinians were threatened with the execution of their families if they didn't comply with the occupation's demands.
Mosques were demolished. The houses of God! As the Quran says: "And who are more unjust than those who prevent the name of Allah from being mentioned in His mosques and strive for their destruction?" Yet, the world remains silent.
The children of Gaza now play "funeral." They have seen so many bodies that they put their toys on stretchers and carry them in mock funeral processions.

Sexual violence and rape are systematically used against men, women, and children.
Muslims are forbidden from praying or fasting. They are forced to throw the Quran on the ground and listen to insults against Islam.
Prisoners are taken as "extra" (bargaining chips) without charge, simply for providing aid to others.
Strip searches occur multiple times a day for men, women, and children. Women are forcibly stripped of their hijabs; those who refuse are killed.
Torture by electricity continues until the prisoner faints or bleeds.
Forced Prostration: Prisoners are forced to sit in a "prostration" (Sujood) position—without being allowed to pray—for more than 18 hours a day.
The One-Minute Rule: Prisoners are given only one minute every three days to use the bathroom/wash. If they are a second late, they and their entire cell are brutally punished.
Sensory Torture: Prisoners cannot sleep due to constant noise, provocation, and the sounds of dogs and guards' boots. They endure this with no food, no water, and no hygiene.

A Call to Action
The "Death Penalty Law" is not a new development; it is just a legal label for a reality that has existed for years. It is a test of our patience—a patience that should have already turned into waves of rage to save what can be saved.
Do not extinguish the last glimmer of hope that thousands cling to. Speak up. Do not be silent.

comments.author: @pweddy1
comments.text:
The reality is while we are “all different”, we share a common biology.   This overarching biology might be disrupted by years of eating fruit loops and other non nutritional “foods” but we all share the same core architecture.  We have differences in our taste and willpower, as a diabetic I’ve had several people ask me, when they were diagnosed as a type 2 diabetic, what to do and the most common response is oh I can’t give up pasta or insert favorite food.

I used to cook pasta multiple times a week every week when I get home from work. When they told me to cut out fat and red meat, I started eating healthy foods like “baked potatoes.”  Then they diagnosed me as a diabetic, and I realized everything they told me was wrong.  I mean, the medical professionals that were treating me.

The medical standard of care before the intervention of insulin therapy was a low-carb diet for diabetes.   The very first diabetic education class I took 20 years ago told me that and they also told me but people can’t control themselves so we just give them a pill.  They told me this right after I was prescribed metformin.

Maybe you can be healthy on an all carb diet, but I doubt it.  Your body can produce glucose if it needs it through the process of gluconeogenesis that’s a huge problem for me now as a type two diabetic because my blood sugar doesn’t come back down when that happens.  It can’t produce amino acids or fatty acids.   I think in a long-term study meat wins.  Because your body can’t produce what you get from it, maybe you don’t need to go full carnivore but you should probably leave out anything that’s man-made and doesn’t come from nature.

As a biochemist, ‘the amino acids become entangled so they’re harder to break down’ is just such an absurd statement. The ‘entanglement’ is referring to to denaturation, the loss of a protein’s ordered secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structure, thus becoming ‘scrambled’ as the chemical bonds holding the protein’s ‘shape’ have been broken. comments.text:
Hey! Love your videos. I'm really late to the party on this one, but i did want to comment on raw milk:

As long as you are familiar with your source, and know they take better care of their cows, ie: their hygiene, their health, cleanliness of living conditions, free access to outdoors, raw milk is actually really good for you! Unfortunately, the high heat pasteurization process kills and removes almost all the vital nutrients(and good bacteria) of milk. Then they "fortify" it, watering it down, and, depending on the type, removing fat. Also, remember why pasteurization came around. It was because of the poor conditions cows were living in when mass production came around. It created unhealthy environments for bad bacteria to be created in and consumed by the cows. Before that, everyone drank raw milk, sometimes right from the teat. Raw milk from a reputable source is by far healthier. 

It also tastes WAY better. I hated milk growing up, and once i tried raw milk, i realized why. Its because pasteurized, highly processed milk is a far cry from the real stuff. 

As Ron Swanson says, "there's only one more thing i hate more than lying. Skim milk. Which is water that's lying about being milk." 😂

Do your proper research and make the best decision for yourself first, but don't knock it until you try it! 

*Another note: there are also people who process fibrous foods waaaay too quickly, like me. Its like the fiber kicks the digestive system into high gear. So a lot of times, the food is out of our systems before it has a chance to properly digest and utilize any nutrients, leaving you feeling groggy, tired, and still hungry. However, meat is super slow digesting. Since it is so dense, it slows down your digestion, giving your body time to properly break it down, absorb nutrients, and therefore, feel fuller longer. And i will do anything to feel fuller longer, so i do tend to lead to a higher meat and protein diet. One of my meal preps is a meat heavy chili with beans, and other cooked veggies. Cooked veggies have also shown to digest slower than raw, so I stay away from the leaf type salads unless i am eating a big steak with it. Long story short, that is probably why those out there who try a carnivore/animal based diet tend to have so much success, and they feel so much better than they did on the standard american diet(sad). So they want to share that with everyone they know. Problem is, with social media, that is literally everyone. And everyone has their own opinion, lol.
